questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the right way to think about documenting one architecture for multiple audiences?
options: Each audience reads at a different altitude, and the architect should produce the right altitude of document for each one rather than one document serving everyone
Write one comprehensive document and hand it to every audience unchanged
Only executives need documentation; developers can read the code directly
Admins should receive the same document as the CTA Review Board
questions.explain: The lesson's central idea is that different audiences need genuinely different documents at different altitudes — not a single document trimmed or expanded, but content and framing matched to each reader's real question.

questions.q: What is an executive sponsor's 'real question,' per this lesson, as distinguished from a developer's?
options: Which Apex class implements the retry policy
Is this safe to invest in, and what could still go wrong?
What exact fields are mapped in the integration
What error code appears in the Sync_Error_Log__c object
questions.explain: An executive's real question is about investment safety and remaining risk, not implementation detail — which is why an executive summary (Lesson 11) answers it in a sentence or two, not a field-level mapping.

questions.q: In the worked billing-sync example, why are the executive, developer, and admin documents described as NOT being three versions of the same content?
options: Because they describe three unrelated integrations
Because only the developer document is considered real documentation
Because each one is written at its own altitude using only the detail relevant to that reader's real question, not a trimmed-down or expanded copy of a single master document
Because the admin document intentionally contains false information to simplify it
questions.explain: All three describe the same underlying integration, but each is purpose-built for its reader's actual question — compressing, including, or framing detail differently rather than being edited versions of one source document.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the most frequent documentation mistake?
options: Writing too many diagrams for a single document
Using Mermaid instead of Lucidchart
Including an executive summary in a Solution Design Document
Documentation written at the wrong altitude for its actual reader — e.g., handing a developer-level document to an executive
questions.explain: The lesson specifically names wrong-altitude documentation — not missing documentation — as the most common failure: detail-heavy content reads as noise to an executive, and a one-sentence summary is useless to a developer who needs to build the retry logic.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect matching documentation altitude to audience with the Salesforce CTA Review Board?
options: It notes that recognizing and producing the right altitude for a given reader is exactly the kind of communication judgment a Review Board panel watches for when a candidate presents and defends a design
It claims the Review Board only ever reads one document from each candidate and never asks questions
It claims the Review Board does not evaluate communication skill at all, only technical correctness
It states that CTA candidates are exempt from needing an executive summary
questions.explain: The lesson ties the skill of matching altitude to audience directly to what a Review Board panel is watching for during a candidate's live presentation and Q&A, since the board evaluates reasoning and communication, not just a finished design.
